back2basics.concept: Representation of the People Act and Electoral Roll Management
back2basics.text: The Representation of the People Act governs the preparation and revision of electoral rolls in India. It designates specific officials such as the Chief Electoral Officer and Electoral Registration Officers as authorities responsible for maintaining accurate voter lists. Electoral rolls are periodically revised to add eligible voters and remove ineligible or duplicate entries, ensuring free and fair elections. The Act does not recognize judicial or tribunal bodies as authorities for electoral roll decisions unless specifically empowered.

2026-10-31-am-028fa3234a.deck: The Election Commission of India filed appeals against the inclusion of 16.10 lakh voters in West Bengal whose names had been cleared by judicial officers during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. This raises constitutional and legal issues about the authority of officials to file such appeals under the Representation of the People Act.

body.label: Judicial clearance of voters
body.text: During the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR), judicial officers cleared 16.10 lakh voters whose names had earlier been flagged for logical discrepancies.

body.label: Authorized officials under the Act
body.text: The Representation of the People Act recognizes the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), District Electoral Officer (DEO), Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), and Assistant Electoral Registration Officer (AERO) as the authorities responsible for electoral rolls.

body.label: Dispute over appellants' authority
body.text: The appeals were filed by 'officers of the office of CEO West Bengal' but it is unclear if these were the authorized officials since the Act does not mention any appellate tribunals created by the Supreme Court.

body.label: Supreme Court's role
body.text: The Supreme Court formed Appellate Tribunals during its supervision of the SIR to adjudicate disputed cases, but these tribunals are not recognized authorities under the Act.

sections.heading: Who has the authority to manage electoral rolls and file appeals?

body.label: Scope of SIR
body.text: The SIR involved reviewing roughly 60 lakh 'doubtful and pending' voter cases in West Bengal.

body.label: Judicial officers' decisions
body.text: Judicial officers cleared 32,77,360 voters and rejected 27.23 lakh, of which 22 lakh appealed to the Appellate Tribunals.

body.label: Bulk appeals and pending cases
body.text: Alongside individual appeals, 16,10,311 bulk appeals challenged the inclusion of voters restored by judicial officers, resulting in over 38 lakh cases pending in the tribunals.

body.label: Election outcome
body.text: West Bengal recorded a historic voter turnout of 92.47% in the Assembly elections held after the SIR process.

2026-10-31-am-091bbf8c0c.anchor: Judicial interpretation of consent and rape laws

back2basics.text: Consent means voluntary agreement to engage in a sexual act. Rape law criminalizes sexual acts without consent, including those obtained by coercion or deception. Courts distinguish between genuine lack of consent and regret after consensual acts, ensuring that the law protects bodily autonomy without being misused.

2026-10-31-am-091bbf8c0c.deck: The Supreme Court ruled that sexual acts consensually entered into cannot be retrospectively branded as rape after a relationship ends. This judgment clarifies the distinction between consent obtained by deception and regret after consensual intimacy, which is crucial for understanding rape laws and consent in India.

body.text: The Court emphasized that rape is a heinous, under-reported crime that strikes at bodily autonomy and must be pursued vigorously when facts show real sexual violence.

body.label: Balancing justice
body.text: The ruling seeks to balance protecting victims of sexual assault with preventing the justice system from becoming a tool of vengeance in failed relationships.

sections.heading: Why does this ruling matter for law and society?

body.text: The case involved a man accused of repeated rape during a seven-year relationship that ended, where the complainant alleged deception about his marital status.

body.label: Court's observation
body.text: The Court observed that physical intimacy during a consensual relationship cannot be retrospectively branded as rape merely because the relationship ended.

back2basics.text: Scheduled banks are those included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and meet certain criteria set by the RBI. They include commercial banks and cooperative banks that comply with RBI regulations. Lending rates are the interest rates banks charge on loans, while deposit rates are the interest paid to depositors. The Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) is a benchmark lending rate that banks use to set interest rates on loans. These rates reflect monetary policy transmission and influence economic activity.

back2basics.text: Social security refers to protection provided by society to individuals to ensure access to healthcare and income security during old age, unemployment, sickness, or other vulnerabilities. Informal sector workers, including unorganised, gig, and platform workers, often lack formal employment benefits, making targeted welfare schemes necessary to bridge this gap.

2026-10-31-am-26701c9b93.deck: The Ministry of Labour & Employment has officially constituted the National Social Security Board for Unorganised Workers and Gig & Platform Workers under the Labour Codes. This board aims to design and monitor welfare schemes for millions of informal sector workers, marking a shift towards integrating gig and platform workers into formal social security frameworks.

body.label: Board constitution
body.text: The Board is established under the Code on Social Security and includes representatives from Central and State Governments, aggregator companies, employers, civil society, workers' unions, and gig & platform associations.

body.label: Leadership and meetings
body.text: It is presided over by the Union Minister for Labour & Employment and meets at least thrice a year following prescribed rules of procedure.

body.label: Functions
body.text: The Board recommends welfare schemes, advises on administration of the Code, monitors social welfare schemes, reviews record-keeping and expenditure, and performs other government-assigned functions.

sections.heading: What is the National Social Security Board for Unorganised, Gig & Platform Workers?

body.label: Addressing informal workforce needs
body.text: It marks a historic shift by formally integrating digital gig and platform workers into India's social security framework alongside traditional unorganised workers.

body.label: Social security gap
body.text: Despite claims of increased social security coverage from 19% in 2015 to 64.3% in 2025, over 92% of India's workforce in unorganised and gig sectors remain largely uncovered.

body.label: Federal concerns
body.text: Labour being a Concurrent List subject requires cooperation between Union and States, but the Board's highly centralised structure with limited State and opposition trade union representation may hinder optimal outcomes.

sections.heading: Why does the National Social Security Board matter for workers and governance?

body.label: Unaddressed past recommendations

body.label: Committee formation
body.text: The Government of India formed the committee to review the banking sector and recommend reforms to make it globally competitive, financially inclusive, and resilient for Viksit Bharat 2047.

body.label: Leadership and members
body.text: Shri Suresh N. Patel, former Central Vigilance Commissioner, chairs the committee, with members including Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu (Deputy Governor, RBI), Smt. Padmaja Chunduru (Former MD & CEO, Indian Bank), and Shri N S Vishwanathan (Former Deputy Governor, RBI).

body.label: Tenure and secretariat
body.text: The committee has a tenure of six months, with the Joint Secretary (Banking), Department of Financial Services, serving as the Member Secretary.

sections.heading: What is the High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat?

body.label: Assess banking practices
body.text: Evaluate current banking practices and prudential norms, identify global best practices, and adapt them for the Indian banking system to create globally competitive banks.

body.label: Review regulatory frameworks
body.text: Examine existing regulatory and legal frameworks for banks, including Regional Rural Banks and Cooperative Banks, to suggest reforms that improve efficiency and ease of banking.

body.label: Capital and credit growth
body.text: Assess long-term capital needs for banks, Development Financial Institutions, and Non-Banking Financial Companies, recommending funding sources and mechanisms to support credit growth.

body.label: Boost private investment
body.text: Analyze differences in cost of capital for businesses and suggest policy options to encourage private investment for sustainable economic growth.

body.label: AI and digital innovation
body.text: Develop a roadmap for AI and digital innovation in banking, including safeguards against cyber risks.

body.label: Talent and capacity building
body.text: Propose strategies for talent acquisition and capacity building to prepare a future-ready banking workforce.

body.label: Review priority schemes
body.text: Evaluate the Priority Sector Lending framework and Lead Bank Scheme for their relevance, effectiveness, and coordination in promoting inclusive and data-driven credit delivery.

body.label: Additional recommendations
body.text: Make recommendations on any other matters referred by the Government of India.

body.label: Overall credit growth
body.text: Non-food bank credit grew by 19.1% year-on-year as of September 30, 2026, compared to 11.2% in the previous year.

body.label: Agriculture credit
body.text: Credit to agriculture and allied activities increased by 19.5% year-on-year, up from 8.9% in the previous year.

body.label: Industry credit
body.text: Credit to industry also grew by 19.5% year-on-year, with large and medium industries accelerating and micro and small industries showing steady growth.

body.label: Key industries
body.text: Major industries like infrastructure, basic metal and metal products, engineering, chemical products, food processing, and textiles showed buoyant credit growth.

body.label: Services sector credit
body.text: Credit to services grew by 28.3% year-on-year, supported by segments such as NBFCs, trade, commercial real estate, transport operators, and professional services.

body.label: Personal loans growth
body.text: Personal loans grew by 17.3% year-on-year, with housing and vehicle loans remaining resilient, advances against fixed deposits accelerating, while loans against gold jewellery and education decelerated but stayed strong.
